title: Adam's Story: Coming Out
description: Adam as an openly gay teenager, his secret relationship with Josh, and the destructive power of internalised homophobia.
content_html:
Adam Bridgeman: Openly Gay

Adam Bridgeman is Dante's sixteen-year-old younger brother and one of the novel's two co-narrators. From the novel's opening, Adam is openly gay. He is not hiding his identity from his family or from the world. He has known he was gay since he was thirteen and, as he states in the novel, he likes it: "I've known I was gay since I was thirteen. And what's more, I like it." This is not a secret whispered in private. It is a statement of self-knowledge and, ultimately, self-acceptance.

Adam faces bullying at school specifically because he is openly gay. The bullying is not triggered by the discovery of a hidden secret — it is a response to the fact that he has refused to hide who he is. Blackman uses Adam's storyline to examine the social cost of being openly different in an environment that punishes difference. Adam's challenge is not concealment. It is survival.

Key Fact

Adam is openly gay. He is out at school and his family are aware or come to be aware of his sexuality. The bullying he faces is the result of a hostile environment responding to his openness — not the result of his secret being exposed.

Josh: The Secret Relationship

Within the novel, Adam enters into a secret relationship with Josh — one of Dante's friends. This relationship is at the heart of the most important thematic threads in the book. But it is essential to understand what kind of relationship this is.

Josh is deeply closeted and ashamed. He is not comfortable with his sexuality. He cannot accept that he is gay, and he cannot accept that he is in a relationship with Adam. The relationship is conducted entirely in secret — at Josh's insistence. Adam must not tell anyone. They must not be seen together. Josh controls the terms of their relationship, and those terms are dictated by his own internalised homophobia.

For Adam, this is painful. He is open. He has accepted himself. He is now in a relationship with someone who is ashamed of him — and ashamed of himself. The contrast between Adam's openness and Josh's shame is one of Blackman's most precise and devastating character constructions.

Internalised homophobia is the process by which someone absorbs society's negative attitudes towards gay people and applies them to themselves. Josh has grown up in a social world — Dante's friend group — where homophobia is casual and accepted. He cannot imagine being openly gay and surviving in that world. Rather than questioning the world, Josh questions himself: he is ashamed of his attraction to Adam, ashamed of the relationship, and desperate to prove to himself and others that he is not gay. This shame, left unaddressed, becomes the engine of violence.

Josh Is Not a Symbol of Acceptance

It would be a fundamental misreading of the novel to describe Josh as a symbol of acceptance or normality in Adam's life. Josh does not prove that Adam's sexuality is natural and healthy. Josh is not a positive presence. He is a source of shame, secrecy, and ultimately catastrophic violence.

Josh's function in the novel is precisely the opposite of acceptance: he embodies the damage that internalised homophobia inflicts — first on himself, and then on Adam. Their relationship does not offer Adam moments of uncomplicated happiness. It offers a connection that must be concealed, built on the foundation of Josh's self-loathing. When that self-loathing reaches its crisis point, the consequences for Adam are devastating.

Key Fact

Josh is not a symbol of acceptance. He is deeply closeted, ashamed of his own sexuality, and insists the relationship remain hidden. His arc demonstrates the destructive effects of internalised homophobia — not the validation of Adam's identity.

The Setup for the Attack

Later in the novel, at a party following Dante's eighteenth birthday at a pub called the Bar Belle, Adam is outed. The exposure of Adam's sexuality in a social context — in front of Dante's friends — creates the conditions for what follows.

It is later revealed that Logan — another of Dante's friends — engineers the attack as a test: Josh must prove he is not gay. The logic is vicious. Josh, closeted and desperate to protect himself, participates. He does not protect Adam. He becomes one of Adam's attackers. This is covered fully in Lesson 5, but it is important to establish here the trajectory that Josh's internalised homophobia sets in motion.

Blackman structures the contrast between Adam and Josh very precisely. Adam is openly gay and faces the external consequences of that openness — bullying, hostility, social isolation. Josh is closeted and faces the internal consequences of that concealment — shame, self-denial, violence. Blackman suggests that the external hostility Adam faces and the internal destruction Josh experiences are both products of the same homophobic environment. The novel does not ask which is worse. It shows how the same poison kills in different ways.

Blackman's Authorial Purpose

Blackman, who was Children's Laureate from 2013 to 2015, has spoken about her reasons for writing this novel. She wanted to explore masculinity, identity, and the cost of conformity — particularly for young men who are told, implicitly or explicitly, that there are things they cannot be if they want to be accepted. Adam's storyline is her most direct examination of the cost of homophobia: not just for those who face it from outside, but for those who have absorbed it inside themselves.

The novel was published in 2010, before marriage equality in England and Wales (which came in 2014). The social context it describes — in which being openly gay as a teenager means sustained bullying and risk of violence — was and remains real. Blackman chose not to soften this reality. Adam's experience is presented without false resolution: being openly gay does not protect him from violence. But it also does not break him.
exam_tip_html: When writing about Adam's character, be precise about what 'openly gay' means in the context of the novel. Examiners will reward students who can explain that Adam's challenge is not self-discovery or concealment but survival in a hostile environment. When writing about Josh, be clear that his function is to explore internalised homophobia — his relationship with Adam is defined by shame and secrecy, and his arc leads to violence, not acceptance.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Adam is openly gay from the novel's opening — he faces bullying because he is out, not because he is hiding something.
  • Josh is Adam's secret boyfriend, but the relationship is defined by Josh's internalised homophobia: he insists on secrecy and is ashamed of Adam and of himself.
  • Josh is not a symbol of acceptance — his arc demonstrates the destructive consequences of internalised homophobia and leads directly to the novel's violent climax.
  • Blackman contrasts Adam's openness with Josh's secrecy to show that the same homophobic environment kills in different ways: through external hostility and internal destruction.

practice_questions.text: How does Blackman present Adam as an openly gay teenager navigating a hostile social environment? You should consider the context in which the novel was written.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (21-25): Perceptive analysis of Adam's openness and its consequences. Discusses: his statement of self-knowledge ('I've known I was gay since I was thirteen'), the fact that bullying is a response to his openness not his concealment, the emotional cost of survival in a homophobic environment. Context: homophobia in schools in early 21st-century Britain, Blackman's Children's Laureate role, the novel published pre-marriage equality (2010). Comments on Blackman's decision not to soften the reality Adam faces.
Top band (16-20): Clear analysis with relevant evidence.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some explained points.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Basic response.
Lower band (1-5): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: Explore how Blackman uses Josh's character to explore the theme of internalised homophobia.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (21-25): Perceptive exploration of internalised homophobia. Discusses: Josh's shame about his own sexuality, his insistence on secrecy, the contrast with Adam's openness, how Josh's self-loathing drives the violence of the attack. Context: peer pressure, masculinity norms, the social environment in which both characters grew up. Comments on Blackman's structural use of Josh as a vehicle for examining what repression does to people.
Top band (16-20): Clear discussion with evidence.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some relevant analysis.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Limited points.
Lower band (1-5): Minimal response.

practice_questions.text: "Adam's greatest challenge in the novel is not his sexuality but the world's response to it." How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (21-25): Convincing argument. Agrees: Adam has accepted himself ('I've known I was gay since I was thirteen. And what's more, I like it.'); his challenge is external hostility, not internal conflict. Complicates: the relationship with Josh shows that even Adam's closest intimate relationship is defined by another person's shame — so the 'world' reaches inside his private life. Concludes: Adam's identity is not the problem; the problem is the social environment, which includes the people he trusts.
Top band (16-20): Balanced argument.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some engagement.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Limited discussion.
Lower band (1-5): Minimal response.

practice_questions.text: How does Blackman use the contrast between Adam and Josh to explore different responses to a homophobic environment?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (21-25): Perceptive structural analysis. Discusses: Adam openly gay, Josh closeted; Adam accepts himself, Josh is consumed by shame; Adam faces external hostility, Josh faces internal destruction; both are products of the same homophobic environment. Comments on Blackman's technique of juxtaposing the two characters to show the full cost of homophobia.
Top band (16-20): Clear comparison with evidence.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some relevant contrasts.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Basic comparison.
Lower band (1-5): Simple points.

practice_questions.text: How does Blackman create sympathy for Adam in the chapters narrated from his perspective?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (21-25): Perceptive analysis of narrative technique. Discusses: first-person narration giving direct access to Adam's feelings and reasoning; his self-knowledge and self-acceptance making him a morally clear character even as others judge him; the gap between how he sees himself and how his environment treats him; the painful dynamic of a relationship in which his boyfriend is ashamed of him. Blackman's authorial intent to challenge reader prejudice.
Top band (16-20): Clear discussion.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some relevant points.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Basic response.
Lower band (1-5): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Blackman present the social pressures that shape the behaviour of young men in the novel?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (21-25): Perceptive analysis of social context. Discusses: Josh's shame as a product of peer group norms, Logan's engineering of the attack as a 'test' of masculinity, Dante's world of male friendship built on conformity. Context: masculinity, peer pressure, the silence around male vulnerability that the novel's title refers to. Blackman's argument that social pressure produces violence.
Top band (16-20): Clear contextual discussion.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some relevant points.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Basic response.
Lower band (1-5): Minimal response.

knowledge_checks.q: Adam's sexuality in the novel: which statement is correct?
options: Adam is openly gay from the novel's opening and faces bullying because he is out
Adam is hiding his sexuality from his family throughout the novel
Adam gradually comes out during the course of the novel
Adam is not openly gay until after the attack

knowledge_checks.q: Which statement best describes Josh's relationship with Adam?
options: Josh is supportive and open about their relationship
Josh is Adam's best friend who helps him come out
Josh is Adam's secret boyfriend who insists the relationship remain hidden due to his own shame
Josh encourages Adam to be more open about his sexuality

knowledge_checks.q: Josh's function in the novel is to demonstrate the destructive effects of _____.
Adam states: 'I've known I was gay since I was thirteen. And what's more, I _____.'
Match each description to the correct character:
right: Openly gay, faces bullying because he refuses to hide his identity
Closeted and ashamed, insists the relationship with Adam remain secret
Engineers the homophobic attack as a 'test' for Josh to prove he is not gay

flashcard_questions.q: How does Adam describe his own sexuality in the novel?
flashcard_questions.a: 'I've known I was gay since I was thirteen. And what's more, I like it.' He is openly gay from the start.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does Adam face bullying at school?
flashcard_questions.a: Because he is openly gay — the bullying is a response to his openness, not to the discovery of a secret.

flashcard_questions.q: Who is Josh, and what is his relationship with Adam?
flashcard_questions.a: Josh is one of Dante's friends and Adam's secret boyfriend — but he is closeted, ashamed, and insists the relationship remain hidden.

flashcard_questions.q: Is Josh a symbol of acceptance and normality for Adam?
flashcard_questions.a: No. Josh is defined by internalised homophobia. He is ashamed of the relationship, demands secrecy, and ultimately becomes one of Adam's attackers.
The process of absorbing society's negative attitudes towards gay people and applying them to oneself — Josh's shame about his own sexuality is the central example.

flashcard_questions.q: What contrast does Blackman create between Adam and Josh?
flashcard_questions.a: Adam is openly gay and faces external hostility; Josh is closeted and faces internal destruction. Both are products of the same homophobic environment.

flashcard_questions.q: When was Boys Don't Cry published, and what is the significance of the date?
flashcard_questions.a: 2010 — before marriage equality in England and Wales (2014). The social context Adam navigates was a real and present reality.

flashcard_questions.q: What was Blackman's role from 2013 to 2015?
flashcard_questions.a: Children's Laureate — appointed three years after Boys Don't Cry was published.

glossary_terms.definition: Not concealing one's sexual orientation — publicly self-identified. Adam is openly gay from the novel's opening.
The acceptance of negative social attitudes about one's own sexual orientation, applying society's prejudice to oneself. Josh's shame is the novel's main example.
Concealing one's sexual orientation from others, often due to fear of social consequences or shame.
Having one's sexual orientation publicly revealed without consent — what happens to Adam at the party.
Continuing to exist and function despite hostile conditions — Adam's challenge throughout the novel.
